items.why: The negation cleanly distinguishes persisting in evil from appointing priests again.
“He” and “gives” blur the old prophet, the man of God, and the Lord as possible sources.
It clearly distinguishes Jonathan’s single victory from the four collectively defeated by David and his men.
Resolving “him” to the doubting officer rather than the man of God is clear and consequential.
It precisely separates the sons who saddle the donkey from the old prophet who mounts it.
The question sharply distinguishes the first covenant’s three parties from the following two-party covenant.
Uzziah’s burial is followed explicitly by Jotham’s meaningful royal succession.
The explicit “because” identifies divine affliction, not the priests’ actions, as Uzziah’s reason.
The imagined sequence is recoverable, but the stem fails to signal that it is only the king’s theory.
It clearly tests the men’s decisive choice of surrender over the fatal city and gate alternatives.
“Who kills first” tests little beyond the arbitrary narrative order of two separate battles.
“The news” is a circular, contentless key to the opaque question “What is later reported?”
The command’s pronoun clearly refers to the man of God, though the competing self-capture reading is weak.
It cleanly distinguishes Uzziah, who enters first, from Azariah, who follows him.
The two quoted days provide a stable distinction between the women’s respective children.
It directly distinguishes Zechariah’s instruction from Amaziah’s example.
“In reply to the doubt” precisely selects Elisha’s warning rather than his earlier price prophecy.
The refusal’s explicit divine-command rationale is central and clearly excludes dissatisfaction with the offer.
The answer is textually adjacent to Paul’s departure, but the immediate-sequence boundary is fairly mechanical.
It tests an arbitrary ordering of mobilizing, marching, and besieging rather than an important distinction.
It clearly separates Jehoiada as giver from David as the weapons’ former owner.
The accusers’ role is clear, but the metatextual word “addressee” makes the stem unnecessarily forced.
It usefully distinguishes the people’s purpose—making Uzziah king—from the circumstance of Amaziah’s death.
It tests the important command hierarchy between the 2,600 leaders and the officials who conducted the muster.
The pronoun sequence clearly makes the traveling man of God, not the assisting prophet, the lion’s victim.
It duplicates Q89C41’s trampling fact while stating the officer’s role almost outright.
The phrase “for the king” isolates the off-duty companies despite the nearby on-duty assignments.
The letter heading clearly distinguishes sender from recipient, though it is a very direct lookup.
Abishai’s rescue of David makes Ishbi-Benob the unambiguous and significant victim.
It clearly contrasts the men’s new plan to report the news with their earlier concealment of goods.
Paul’s quoted wording unambiguously assigns the message to the young man rather than himself.
The reporting does immediately precede the plunder, but the question mainly tests a narrow sequence boundary.
It meaningfully resolves “he loved the soil” to Uzziah rather than to his field workers.
The speaker’s first-person account clearly identifies her own son as the child eaten first.
It sharply separates the king who requests prayer from the man of God who intercedes.
It distinguishes the three peoples opposed with God’s help from the tribute-paying Ammonites, though grading the list may vary.
“First” is awkward because the body is laid on the donkey before being taken to the city and then the tomb.
It tests the central identity of the rescued heir rather than confusing him with his dead father.
The explicit causal clause attributes the city’s calm to Athaliah’s death, not merely to public rejoicing.
It cleanly distinguishes the two centurions receiving the order from the soldiers they must prepare.
It separates the supposed attackers from the Israelite king believed to have hired them.
The sender-versus-messenger wording makes the king the clear referent of “this murderer.”
“According to the claim” correctly scopes the lie and identifies the man of God as the intended guest.
The passage explicitly links Paul’s prolonged speech to his planned departure the next day.
The contrast is recoverable, but “soldiers” is broad enough to include the cavalry that continues onward.
The plural pronouns clearly identify Sceva’s seven sons as those beaten and driven from the house.
The forced “items’ arrival” phrasing simply cues the exact word “left,” encouraging word spotting.
It clearly distinguishes the commander who must transport Paul from the council requesting his appearance.
Burning follows assembly directly, but “materials” is generic and the immediate-order test is mechanical.
The woman is also taken out and executed, leaving “who is ordered” less stable than the key assumes.
It clearly distinguishes the noise that prompts Athaliah’s movement from the king she sees only afterward.
The explicit statement that the plotters await the commander’s consent establishes the required condition.
The warning is directly addressed to the man of God, clearly excluding the old prophet who delivers it.
The prophecy clearly names Josiah as the future killer rather than Jeroboam, who is merely present.
